Excess mortality

Source: vignettes/excess-mortality.Rmd
excess-mortality.Rmd

Excess deaths are the deaths observed in a period of crisis (a heatwave, an epidemic, a war) minus the deaths expected without it. The expected deaths are not observed; they come from a model of the years before the crisis, the baseline. mt_excess() fits any mortality model of the package to the baseline years, forecasts the later years with the observed exposures, and compares the observed deaths with each simulated path of expected deaths. The intervals therefore contain the uncertainty of the baseline trend and the random variation of the death counts. The WHO estimates of the excess mortality of the COVID-19 pandemic follow this approach with their own baseline model (Msemburi et al. 2023).

The results are

  • the excess: observed minus expected deaths;
  • the P-score: the excess in percent of the expected deaths;
  • p_positive: the share of paths in which the observed deaths exceed the expected deaths;

by year, and optionally by age group, stratum, and summed over years.

The heatwave of August 2003 in France

Deaths and exposures of France (Human Mortality Database, via the demography package), single years of age to 100+. The baseline is a Lee-Carter model of the years 1990-2002:

library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
fr <- as_mt_data(demography::fr.mort)
x <- mt_regroup(mt_subset(fr, periods = c(1990, 2006)), age = 0:100)
fit <- mt_fit(lee_carter(), mt_subset(x, periods = c(1990, 2002)))
ex <- mt_excess(fit, x, by = character(), seed = 1)
ex[, list(period, observed, expected_q0.5, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975, p_score_q0.5)]
#>    period observed expected_q0.5 excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975
#>     <num>    <num>         <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>
#> 1:   2003   552339      537269.0      5606.375     15070.0     25445.525
#> 2:   2004   509429      539842.5    -44524.750    -30413.5    -16279.675
#> 3:   2005   527535      543595.0    -33115.700    -16060.0       798.525
#> 4:   2006   516416      548697.5    -52128.375    -32281.5    -13218.850
#>    p_score_q0.5
#>           <num>
#> 1:     2.804926
#> 2:    -5.633773
#> 3:    -2.954405
#> 4:    -5.883296

by = character() sums women and men. In 2003, about 15,000 more people died than expected (95% interval 5,600 to 25,400), 2.8% more than expected. Fouillet et al. (2006) counted about 15,000 excess deaths between 1 and 20 August 2003 against the mortality of 2000-2002, so the rest of the year was close to the baseline.

mt_plot_excess(ex)

The years after 2003 lie below the baseline: 30,000 fewer deaths than expected in 2004 and as many in 2006. Part of the deficit of 2004 may be deaths brought forward by the heatwave, but the deficit continues: from 2003 mortality fell faster than the trend of 1990-2002. A baseline extrapolated over several years becomes uncertain, and so do excess deaths far from the baseline period.

By sex and age group:

mt_excess(fit, x, periods = 2003, seed = 1)[, list(sex, observed, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975)]
#>       sex observed excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975
#>    <char>    <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>
#> 1: female   273315      3448.800     11671.5     19341.575
#> 2:   male   279024     -1337.075      3531.0      8953.625
ex_age <- mt_excess(fit, x, periods = 2003, by = character(), ages = c(0, 45, 65, 75, 85), seed = 1)
ex_age[, list(age, observed, excess_q0.5, p_score_q0.025, p_score_q0.5, p_score_q0.975)]
#>       age observed excess_q0.5 p_score_q0.025 p_score_q0.5 p_score_q0.975
#>    <char>    <num>       <num>          <num>        <num>          <num>
#> 1:   0-44    29115      -439.0     -4.4707459    -1.485417      1.3511059
#> 2:  45-64    81495      2498.5      1.5390342     3.162798      4.8867019
#> 3:  65-74    89304     -1400.5     -3.5247795    -1.544025      0.3337944
#> 4:  75-84   167633      5619.0      0.5302193     3.468219      6.3495506
#> 5:    85+   184792      8982.0      3.3076824     5.108924      6.9832477
mt_plot_excess(ex_age, type = "p_score")

Three quarters of the excess were women, and most were 75 and older; the P-score was highest at 85+. Fouillet et al. (2006) also found the excess concentrated among women and at old ages. ages gives the start of each age group; the deaths are summed path by path before the quantiles are taken.

The same comparison on the scale of life expectancy: the observed life expectancy at birth minus that of each path of expected rates.

le <- mt_excess(fit, x, periods = 2003, quantity = "life_expectancy", seed = 1)
le[, list(sex, observed, expected_q0.5, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975)]
#>       sex observed expected_q0.5 excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975
#>    <char>    <num>         <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>
#> 1: female 82.95594      83.20279    -0.5685339  -0.2468486     0.1022864
#> 2:   male 75.87930      76.00291    -0.3828217  -0.1236114     0.0994448

Life expectancy of women was 0.25 years lower than expected; the interval includes zero, because an annual life expectancy hides a shock of two weeks.

The choice of baseline

The baseline is an assumption. A few alternatives, each fitted to the years before 2003:

base <- list("Lee-Carter 1990-2002" = fit,
             "Lee-Carter 1993-2002" = mt_fit(lee_carter(), mt_subset(x, periods = c(1993, 2002))),
             "random walk 1990-2002" = mt_fit(rwd(), mt_subset(x, periods = c(1990, 2002))),
             "Li-Lee 1990-2002" = mt_fit(li_lee(), mt_subset(x, periods = c(1990, 2002))))
rbindlist(lapply(names(base), function(b) {
  mt_excess(base[[b]], x, periods = 2003, by = character(), seed = 1)[, baseline := b]
}))[, list(baseline, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975, p_score_q0.5)]
#>                 baseline excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975 p_score_q0.5
#>                   <char>         <num>       <num>         <num>        <num>
#> 1:  Lee-Carter 1990-2002      4662.100    15269.50      24719.80     2.843114
#> 2:  Lee-Carter 1993-2002      5804.200    15274.50      23506.88     2.844072
#> 3: random walk 1990-2002      6604.257    15194.38      26120.47     2.828732
#> 4:      Li-Lee 1990-2002      -258.550    14395.00      28768.22     2.675929

The medians agree within 900 deaths. Li-Lee, whose common factor ties the trends of women and men together, gives the widest interval of the sum: when the trend errors of the parts are correlated, they do not cancel in the total. Report the baseline model and years with the results, and compare a few.

A large shock: France 1918

The influenza pandemic of 1918 against a baseline of 1900-1913 (ages 0-94 and 95+, because some exposures at the oldest ages are zero in these years):

y <- mt_regroup(mt_subset(fr, periods = c(1900, 1919)), age = 0:95)
e18 <- mt_excess(lee_carter(), y, baseline = c(1900, 1913), seed = 1)
e18[, list(sex, period, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975, p_score_q0.5)]
#>        sex period excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975 p_score_q0.5
#>     <char>  <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>        <num>
#>  1: female   1914    -11119.275     17744.5      47573.07     6.274322
#>  2: female   1915    -21114.825     23712.0      62769.37     8.547329
#>  3: female   1916    -37333.100     18283.5      66942.35     6.812711
#>  4: female   1917    -40205.525     28591.5      77379.35    10.843196
#>  5: female   1918     37314.225    112526.5     172727.88    42.546285
#>  6: female   1919    -31413.825     45546.0     109408.95    17.512169
#>  7:   male   1914    278445.150    305674.5     329615.65    98.833110
#>  8:   male   1915    316801.950    351930.5     381905.85   117.832756
#>  9:   male   1916    202813.575    239698.5     274085.35    83.982005
#> 10:   male   1917    111154.650    159475.0     199189.42    57.155606
#> 11:   male   1918    220695.450    275881.0     322360.60    98.098397
#> 12:   male   1919     -8753.025     54239.5     103360.67    19.707532
mt_plot_excess(e18, type = "p_score")

The excess of men starts in 1914, with the First World War, so for men it mixes war deaths and the pandemic. That of women is concentrated in 1918: 113,000 deaths (95% interval 37,000 to 173,000), 43% more than expected. The intervals widen from 1914 on, because the expected deaths of 1918 are forecast five years ahead of the baseline. By age, for 1918:

e18a <- mt_excess(lee_carter(), y, baseline = c(1900, 1913), periods = 1918, ages = c(0, 15, 45, 65), seed = 1)
e18a[, list(sex, age, observed, excess_q0.5, p_score_q0.5)]
#>       sex    age observed excess_q0.5 p_score_q0.5
#>    <char> <char>    <num>       <num>        <num>
#> 1: female   0-14    56670     25833.5    83.775761
#> 2: female  15-44   102306     55792.0   119.946683
#> 3: female  45-64    71760     14789.5    25.959927
#> 4: female    65+   146271     15674.0    12.001807
#> 5:   male   0-14    60876     25979.0    74.444812
#> 6:   male  15-44   275811    226843.0   463.248014
#> 7:   male  45-64    94349     15915.0    20.290945
#> 8:   male    65+   126074      7537.5     6.358801

Women aged 15-44 died at more than twice the expected rate, a mark of the 1918 pandemic, which was most lethal for young adults.

Germany, 2020-2024, by Land

The German data of the package (Destatis) give deaths by Land, sex and age group. A few small cells are suppressed; mt_fill_suppressed() estimates them from the totals of Germany:

library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
de <- mt_data(deaths = de_deaths[de_deaths$cause == "all", ], population = de_population, by = c("region", "sex"))
de <- mt_as_exposure(de, type = "dec31")
de <- mt_regroup(mt_subset(de, periods = c(2010, 2024)), age = "deaths")
de <- mt_fill_suppressed(de, mt_hierarchy(region = "Deutschland"))
laender <- mt_subset(de, region != "Deutschland", drop = TRUE)

The populations are given by Land, so the national total is formed by summing the Länder (mt_aggregate_strata()). A Lee-Carter model of the national total, both sexes, fitted to 2010-2019:

h <- mt_hierarchy(region = "Deutschland", sex = "both")
germany <- mt_subset(mt_aggregate_strata(laender, h), region == "Deutschland" & sex == "both", drop = TRUE)
ex_de <- mt_excess(lee_carter(), germany, baseline = c(2010, 2019), by = character(), seed = 1)
ex_de[, list(period, observed, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975, p_score_q0.5, p_positive)]
#>    period observed excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975 p_score_q0.5
#>     <num>    <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>        <num>
#> 1:   2020   985572      -963.875     26354.5      54663.78     2.747500
#> 2:   2021  1023687     13959.925     57289.5      97750.07     5.928151
#> 3:   2022  1066341     47014.275    101341.5     145831.95    10.501715
#> 4:   2023  1028206      2275.975     66324.5     124618.85     6.895288
#> 5:   2024  1007758    -32997.600     30685.5      95076.57     3.140555
#>    p_positive
#>         <num>
#> 1:      0.970
#> 2:      0.996
#> 3:      1.000
#> 4:      0.978
#> 5:      0.828
mt_excess(lee_carter(), germany, baseline = c(2010, 2019), by = character(), cumulative = TRUE,
          seed = 1)[, list(from, period, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975)]
#>     from period excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975
#>    <num>  <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>
#> 1:  2020   2020      -963.875     26354.5      54663.78
#> 2:  2020   2021     21745.725     85125.0     145962.10
#> 3:  2020   2022     72705.150    182873.5     284930.35
#> 4:  2020   2023     85289.000    250826.0     401462.32
#> 5:  2020   2024     61848.500    282996.5     483027.62

The excess rose from about 26,000 in 2020 to 101,000 in 2022 and fell afterwards; from 2020 to 2022 it summed to 183,000, with a wide interval (73,000 to 285,000). The interval is wide because the expected deaths of 2022 are a forecast three years beyond a baseline of ten years.

Summing separate models of the 32 strata (Land by sex) instead gives a much narrower interval for the same total:

mt_excess(lee_carter(), laender, baseline = c(2010, 2019), by = character(),
          seed = 1)[, list(period, excess_q0.025, excess_q0.5, excess_q0.975)]
#>    period excess_q0.025 excess_q0.5 excess_q0.975
#>     <num>         <num>       <num>         <num>
#> 1:   2020     11068.050     19094.0      28479.55
#> 2:   2021     35794.700     48118.5      60482.52
#> 3:   2022     76635.350     91800.0     106571.65
#> 4:   2023     36244.150     54795.5      73615.62
#> 5:   2024      1853.475     22284.0      41176.32

Separate models draw their trend errors independently, so these cancel in the sum, while in reality the Länder share much of their trend. For a total, use a model of the total, or a joint model of its parts such as li_lee(), whose common factor carries the shared trend. The warning suppressed here concerns the oldest men of Bremen, a small population.

P-scores of the Länder in 2021, from a Li-Lee model with one common factor per sex:

ex_l <- mt_excess(li_lee(common_by = "sex"), laender, baseline = c(2010, 2019), by = "region", periods = 2021,
                  seed = 1)
ex_l[order(-p_score_q0.5), list(region, p_score_q0.025, p_score_q0.5, p_score_q0.975, cells, skipped)]
#>                     region p_score_q0.025 p_score_q0.5 p_score_q0.975 cells

In 2021 the excess was highest in Thüringen, Sachsen and Sachsen-Anhalt (P-scores 11-15%); in most western Länder the interval contains zero. cells and skipped count the observed cells used and left out: cells whose deaths were estimated (suppressed cells filled above) are not compared unless include_estimated = TRUE.

Do the intervals hold?

When the baseline model describes the years without a shock, the 95% interval of the excess should contain the true excess in 95% of cases. The validation suite of the package checks this on simulated data (mt_example(), a Lee-Carter baseline, deaths at ages 70 and older raised by 10% in two years, 20 replicates): the intervals contained zero where there was no shock in 97.5% of the cases, and the injected deaths in 98% of the cases where there was one. On real data, the coverage depends on how well the baseline model forecasts the years of the shock; a backtest of the baseline model on years without a shock (mt_backtest()) shows how wide its intervals need to be.

References

Acosta RJ, Irizarry RA (2022). A flexible statistical framework for estimating excess mortality. Epidemiology 33(3): 346-353. doi:10.1097/EDE.0000000000001445.

Fouillet A, Rey G, Laurent F, Pavillon G, Bellec S, Guihenneuc-Jouyaux C, Clavel J, Jougla E, Hémon D (2006). Excess mortality related to the August 2003 heat wave in France. International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health 80(1): 16-24. doi:10.1007/s00420-006-0089-4.

Msemburi W, Karlinsky A, Knutson V, Aleshin-Guendel S, Chatterji S, Wakefield J (2023). The WHO estimates of excess mortality associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. Nature 613: 130-137. doi:10.1038/s41586-022-05522-2.
